title: Heaven
hook: less clouds and harps, more being with God and all things made new

segments.voice: Yesterday, purgatory, and how the churches remember their dead. Your line was mercy after death. Whose story did you tell out loud? Day one thousand one hundred seven.

Clouds. Harps. Someone in a white robe at a gate, checking names off a list. The cartoon heaven is so familiar it's hard to see past it. And some of it does come from the Bible: the book of Revelation has harps, and white robes, and gates of pearl. But when the Bible's last pages describe the end of the story, the center of the picture isn't the furniture. It's a person, and one small word that keeps coming back. Today's word: heaven.

Here's how Revelation describes the end: "Behold, the tabernacle of God is with men, and he will dwell with them, and they shall be his people, and God himself shall be with them." With, and with, and with. Then: "God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death." And notice which way things move. Not souls floating up and away, but a holy city coming down, and the one on the throne saying, "Behold, I make all things new." John sees "a new heaven and a new earth": this world healed, not thrown out. The same small word runs through the rest. On the cross, a dying thief says, "Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom." And he hears: "To day shalt thou be with me in paradise." Paul, writing from prison, says he'd like "to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better." And to grieving friends in Thessalonica he says, "and so shall we ever be with the Lord." The churches have their own ways of saying more. Catholics speak of the beatific vision: seeing God face to face. The Orthodox speak of union with God that keeps on deepening, without end. Protestant hymns sing of home, and rest, and the face of Christ. But in these passages the shorthand is simple: heaven is where God is, and the hope they voice is to be with him.
screen: `THE TABERNACLE OF GOD IS WITH MEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold a picture of joy without end. Close your eyes if you like, and let your breathing find its own pace. Bring back one moment of real joy: a table full of people you love, a morning by the sea, a child laughing until they can't stop. Then take away the shadow that often comes with joy, the knowing that it will end. No clock. No goodbyes. Nothing lost. Stay there a while. If you pray, you can thank God for that hope. If you don't, just rest in the shape of it. The bell holds the time.
Heaven. In the Bible's last pages, less a place above the clouds than God living with his people, and all things made new.
Your line: with him. Today, when you're with someone, be fully with them, phone down, for one whole conversation. Day one thousand one hundred seven.

howItsDone: Christians speak of heaven at funerals, in the creeds' "life of the world to come", and in hymns; the Bible's own descriptions come chiefly from Revelation 21–22 and from Jesus's and Paul's promises of being with Christ.

notes: Philippians described as written 'from prison' (Philippians 1:13 'my bonds'); confirm.
The Revelation 21:5 voice is said 'from the throne' (21:5 'he that sat upon the throne said'); confirm.
Church summaries (Catholic beatific vision; Orthodox ever-deepening union; Protestant hymns of home and rest) are brief and uncounted; confirm fairness.
Original οὐρανός: confirm note that the word covers both sky and heaven.

Editor: Revelation 21:5 speaker changed from 'a voice from the throne' to 'the one on the throne' (the KJV has 'he that sat upon the throne said'), in the teach and the match game.

Auditor: garbled "the Bible's own shorthand is short" fixed, and the closing line now reports what the passages say rather than the narrator asserting it. All Revelation 21, Luke 23, Philippians 1:23 and 1 Thessalonians 4:17 quotations checked against the KJV.
